faqs.a: Fixed costs do not change with output: rent, salaries, insurance. Variable costs rise with each unit: materials, packaging, payment fees. The distinction matters because only variable costs affect the contribution margin that pays down fixed costs.
faqs.q: Fixed vs variable costs - what is the difference?

faqs.a: Break-even in revenue is the money target; break-even in units is the sales target. They are the same point expressed differently: break-even revenue = break-even units x price per unit. Use units for operations planning, revenue for financial targets.

Raise the price, cut variable costs, or cut fixed costs. A $1 price rise on a $15 margin cuts break-even by about 7%. Cutting fixed costs helps one-to-one. Beware: raising price may reduce demand, which this simple model does not capture.
faqs.q: How do I lower my break-even point?

faqs.a: Margin of safety = (actual or expected sales - break-even sales) / expected sales. If you expect 5,000 units and break-even is 3,333, your margin of safety is 33% - sales can fall a third before you lose money. Higher is safer.

Yes - use a weighted average contribution margin across products, or calculate break-even revenue = fixed costs / average contribution margin ratio. Single-product break-even is cleaner; with many products, the revenue version is more practical.
faqs.q: Does it work for multiple products?

faqs.a: It means you lose money on every unit before fixed costs, so you can never break even - more sales just mean bigger losses. Raise the price above variable cost, cut variable cost, or stop selling that product.
faqs.q: What if variable cost is higher than price?

break-even-point-calculator.formula:
Contribution margin = price per unit - variable cost per unit.
Break-even units = fixed costs / contribution margin.
Break-even revenue = break-even units x price per unit.
Example: 50,000 / (25 - 10) = 3,333.33 units; revenue = 83,333.33.
howTo: Enter your total fixed costs for the period (rent, salaries, insurance).
Enter your selling price per unit.
Enter the variable cost per unit (materials, packaging, fees).
Read your break-even units, break-even revenue, and contribution margin.
Test scenarios: what happens if costs rise 10% or you discount 5%?
keyFacts: Break-even is the sales level where total revenue exactly covers total costs - zero profit, zero loss.
Contribution margin (price minus variable cost) is what each unit contributes toward fixed costs.
Every unit sold past break-even earns the full contribution margin as profit.
Fixed costs set the hurdle; variable costs set how fast each sale clears it.
Price rises cut break-even fastest, but may reduce demand.
Service businesses use the same maths with billable hours instead of units.

break-even-point-calculator.quickAnswer: Break-even units = fixed costs / (price - variable cost). With $50,000 fixed costs, $25 price, $10 variable cost: contribution margin is $15, break-even is 3,333.33 units, or $83,333.33 in revenue. Every unit past that earns $15 of profit. If your price is below variable cost, you can never break even.

break-even-point-calculator.workedExample:
Fixed costs $50,000, price $25, variable cost $10:
1. Contribution margin = 25 - 10 = $15 per unit.
2. Break-even units = 50,000 / 15 = 3,333.33 units.
3. Break-even revenue = 3,333.33 x 25 = $83,333.33.
4. Check: revenue 83,333.33 - variable costs (3,333.33 x 10 = 33,333.33) - fixed 50,000 = $0. Break-even confirmed.
Sell 3,334 units and you are profitable.
